title: DWP ‘cyber incident’ knocks almost all pensions and benefits systems offline
description:
Department for Work and Pensions officials say welfare payments will continue to be made despite huge outage

text: Almost all pensions and benefits systems in the UK are unavailable after a “cyber incident”.
Anyone trying to check their state pension, make an application for disability benefits or claim universal credit was not able to do so on Friday morning.
Regular benefits and pensions payments are not affected and would continue to be made as normal, the Department for Work and Pension said.
But there were reports from members of the public who said payments they had expected to be in their account had not arrived on Friday morning.
The cause of the incident, and whether it is the result of a cyber-attack, is not publicly known but the department is working with the National Cyber Security Centre.
A range of services were taken down on Thursday as a precautionary measure after “unusual activity” was detected, a government spokesperson said on Friday.

“There is no evidence to suggest that a malicious actor has targeted other government departments and we are working as quickly as possible to establish the facts,” they added. “Currently, there is no evidence of customer data loss but the investigation is ongoing and we are not going to get ahead of that process.”
It comes days after the government issued an alert warning of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks in the UK, particularly against businesses supporting Ukraine.

The incident caused concern among the public, with some reporting problems. One woman, who has two young children, told BBC Radio 4 that she normally receives a universal credit payment on the 27th day of each month and, like others, was concerned about not having enough money to cover bills due to be paid on the first.
“It’s a bit scary because when I called them [the DWP] to ask, they said they couldn’t give me any other information other than the payment would definitely be made by Monday,” she said.

“My weekly shop is on a Sunday so I am having to go into Christmas savings, which I have been saving for the last six or seven months. I am having to pull money out of them to make up for what I don’t have and there are bills coming out also next week.”

The department said in a statement: “We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems. We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption.

“Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links.”

The DWP’s most senior official told a committee of MPs this month that cybersecurity and resilience was one of the issues “that keeps a new permanent secretary awake”.

Sarah Healey, the DWP permanent secretary, was appearing before the work and pensions select committee, where she was asked who would ensure that DWP systems would “not be the frontline in some sort of hybrid warfare from the Kremlin”.

Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries malfunctioned earlier this month, with their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F), in what was blamed on a cyber-attack. The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.
The disruption at the DWP should be a “wake-up call” for the government and public bodies, said Dame Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons science and technology committee.
“People rely on these systems for some of the most essential services the state provides, and they should be able to trust that the tech and data underpinning them are secure and resilient.

“My committee has repeatedly warned that the government cannot achieve its digital transformation of public services without addressing weaknesses in its digital infrastructure and improving standards of data hygiene. Public bodies hold citizens’ data on trust, and that demands the highest standards.”
